'''Samuel Simon Snyder''' (August 18, 1911 &ndash; December 28, 2007<ref name=":2">{{Cite web|title=Computer Pioneers - Samuel S. Snyder|url=https://history.computer.org/pioneers/snyder.html|access-date=2021-06-22|website=history.computer.org}}</ref><ref name=":0">{{Cite web|date=2008-01-17|title=Obituary: Codebreaker, alumnus dies at 96|url=https://www.gwhatchet.com/2008/01/17/obituary-codebreaker-alumnus-dies-at-96/|access-date=2021-06-20|website=The GW Hatchet}}</ref>) was a cryptographer for the United States Government.<ref name="honor" /> His pioneering work in early computers led directly to the development of the computer as we know it, and laid the foundation for many aspects of the modern computing industry.<ref name="honor" /> He is known for having broken every Japanese encrypted message with his partners in the Signal Intelligence Service during World War II and for having developed the [[MARC standards]].<ref name=":0" />

== Career ==
Snyder was an alumnus of [[George Washington University]], where, at the height of the [[Great Depression]], he attended night school, working on various government jobs{{Which|date=June 2021}} during the day.<ref name=":0" /> While still at the university, Snyder started his career in 1934 with the [[Signal Intelligence Service]] as one of the first 10 employees,.<ref name=":0" /><ref name="honor" /> He worked at the National Security Agency until 1964.<ref name=":2" /> He graduated from George Washington University in 1939 with a B.S. in chemistry.<ref name=":0" />

During [[World War II]], Snyder coordinated teams and worked with [[William F. Friedman]] to break Japanese army cryptosystems. He also developed a more systematic approach{{Clarify|date=June 2021}} to using sorting machines for cryptanalysis.<ref name="honor" /> Near the end of the war, he and his partners were able to break every Japanese encrypted message, which, according to the [[National Security Agency]], "is believed to have directly contributed to shortening the war by at least one year".<ref name=":0" /> Snyder also determined whether computers that decoded Axis information at the Signal Intelligence Service were useful for other purposes, and concluded that they were integral to the agency; as a result, the NSA became the "leading computing industry on earth", according to his eldest son.<ref name=":0" />

Later at NSA he worked on one of the early code breaking computers called ABNER<ref>{{cite book |title=Creating the Computer: Government, Industry, and High Technology |author=Kenneth Flamm |pages=[https://archive.org/details/creatingcomputer0000flam/page/81 81] |publisher=Brookings Institution Press |date=1998 |isbn=0815728506 |url=https://archive.org/details/creatingcomputer0000flam/page/81 }}</ref> and other computing systems such as Harvest, one of the earliest general-purpose computers made with IBM.<ref name="honor" /><ref name=":1">{{Cite web|title=ISN 2008/01: [ISN] Samuel Snyder, 96; Broke Codes And Designed|url=http://lists.jammed.com/ISN/2008/01/0008.html|access-date=2021-06-20|website=lists.jammed.com}}</ref> After spending 30 years at the National Security Agency, he worked at the [[Library of Congress]],<ref name="honor" /> where in 1964 he became an information systems specialist.<ref name="honor" /> He was the coordinator of the Library of Congress's information systems from 1964 to 1966.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2" /> There, he helped to create the [[MARC standards]], a machine readable cataloging system that became an international standard electronic database system for libraries and for data sharing in research.<ref name=":0" /><ref name="honor" />

From 1967 to 1970, he worked at the [[Research Analysis Corporation]].<ref name=":2" />

Snyder coauthored the book "Man and the Computer", which was published in 1972 with Ashley Montagu, as well as a classified history of the NSA.

Mr. Snyder was inducted into the [[NSA Hall of Honor]] in 2007,<ref name="honor">{{cite web|author=National Security Agency|date=May 3, 2016|title=Cryptologic Hall of Honor: Samuel S. Snyder|url=https://www.nsa.gov/about/cryptologic-heritage/historical-figures-publications/hall-of-honor/Article/1621844/samuel-s-snyder/|accessdate=2016-11-28}}</ref> and he held a Defense Department [[Meritorious Civilian Service Award]] and The Washington Post's "Ideal Father of the Year" award for 1949.<ref name=":0" />

== Personal life ==
Samuel Snyder married Patricia Yakerson Snyder in 1935; Patricia died in 1996.<ref name=":1" />{{Unreliable source?|date=June 2021}}

He left behind 4 children, 9 grandchildren, and 5 great-grandchildren.<ref name=":0" /> Snyder's eldest son, named Sol and a professor at [[Johns Hopkins School of Medicine]] as of 2008, remembered Samuel Snyder's "knack for math and science" and that he spent his last years "basking in his passion for music".<ref name=":0" /> Sol's elder sister Elaine Hodges (d. 2006) <ref name=":1" />{{Unreliable source?|date=June 2021}}, then 12 years old, described Samuel Snyder as a "mathematician, artist, scientist, house cleaner, sewer, dog harness maker, dog bather, can play the clarinet, saxophone, piccolo, story writer, [and the] best father in the world" in a letter to the Washington Post asking that Snyder be named the Post’s “Ideal Father”; he was awarded that designation in 1949.<ref name=":0" />
